frameworks.name: Work Satisfaction Model
frameworks.definition: A framework for evaluating life satisfaction by distinguishing between work-as-drudgery (driven by external pressure) and work-as-chosen-activity (driven by internal alignment); the critic's frame is projection of their own pain, not objective truth.

claims.text: Most daily work supports a small passion core (roughly 5%); accepting this ratio rather than resisting it sustains high performance without burnout, because the expectation is calibrated to reality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Accepting the 95-5 split prevents the cognitive dissonance and resentment that comes from expecting work to be meaningful 100% of the time.

numbers.axis: proportion of daily work that drives passion

claims.text: Hedonic adaptation means that discovering hypothetically better lifestyle alternatives (travel, new hobbies) would result in temporary satisfaction followed by return to baseline happiness; therefore the search for novelty is not a high-ROI use of time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: New experiences trigger initial pleasure-spike; the nervous system adapts back to baseline within weeks to months; baseline happiness is largely personality-determined and resistant to external change.
bounded_by: Does not apply to people with untreated depression or baseline misery from genuinely harmful circumstances (abusive relationships, dangerous work environments).

claims.text: Critics who say 'you work too much' are projecting their own relationship to work (as drudgery) onto the speaker's choices; the same critic would object to any lifestyle (video games, travel, rest) if their underlying preference is to control how you live.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when the critic does not share the speaker's values or work definition
claims.mechanism: The critic's statement 'I would prefer you live your life the way I want you to live it' reveals that the objection is about control or misaligned values, not rational concern about overwork.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the critic has evidence of actual burnout, health decline, or relationship deterioration caused by work.

claims.text: For someone who genuinely wants their work (rather than being coerced into it), the percentage of time spent working is irrelevant to life satisfaction; the relevant variable is autonomy (ability to choose with whom and what).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the person has genuine choice in work assignment
the work involves collaboration with chosen people
claims.mechanism: Autonomy (choice + control) is the primary driver of life satisfaction; time quantity is a proxy metric that becomes irrelevant when choice is present.
bounded_by: Does not apply when work is coerced, underpaid, or done with people the person would not choose.

claims.text: Hedonistic adaptation and the happiness baseline are resistant enough to external change that the person from a low-happiness culture (example: people in African tribes who never leave) may be as happy as someone in a high-consumption culture; therefore optimizing for experience variety may be misguided.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: assumes no severe deprivation or harm in the comparison groups
claims.mechanism: Happiness setpoint is largely determined by personality traits (neuroticism, extraversion, optimism) and life circumstances; novelty-seeking behavior is individual-variance, not universal path to satisfaction.
bounded_by: Does not apply to situations where 'staying in one place' involves genuinely harmful circumstances (disease, poverty, abuse).

claims.text: Work definition is perception-dependent: the critic interprets work negatively (as burden), so the same activity labeled 'work' is criticized as 'too much', but if relabeled as 'play' (video games all day), the critic would object that the person 'is not working enough'—revealing the criticism is about the label, not the activity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the critic has a negative emotional association with the word 'work'
claims.mechanism: Projection: the critic's objection to the label 'work' reflects their own pain, not objective harm to the target. The same time allocation would be acceptable under a different frame.

examples.text: A family member criticizes the speaker for 'working too much', saying the person should allocate time to travel or try new hobbies like ping pong instead. But the speaker observes: if they stopped work and played video games all day instead, the same critic would say they 'are not working enough'—demonstrating that the objection is to the critic's preferred lifestyle, not to any objective measure of workload.

The speaker lives in Africa serving its tribe and is as happy as Westerners in consumption-based cultures; yet the Western frame assumes that discovering new experiences (travel, hobbies) would deliver satisfaction. The speaker's interpretation: the African example shows that finding more things is not the path to happiness because hedonic adaptation brings all new experiences back to baseline.

practices.text: Do exactly what you want with the highest percentage of your day possible, with the people you want to do it with, and do not optimize for others' projections of how you should live.

When criticized for lifestyle choices by others, identify whether the critic is offering rational concern (health data, relationship impact) or projection of their own values; if projection, acknowledge it ('that is your preference for how I live') and decline to accommodate.

Evaluate work satisfaction by the autonomy available (choice in activity, choice in people) rather than by the time spent; if you have chosen the work and the people, time quantity is a misleading proxy.
